nameStory: The name 'leopard's-bane' comes from an old belief that this plant could ward off or poison leopards and other big cats. The 'bane' part means poison or something that causes harm, reflecting the historical (though likely mistaken) idea that the plant was toxic to these spotted predators.
description: Leopard's-bane is a cheerful yellow wildflower that looks like a bright daisy with a sunny disposition. This perennial plant grows from underground stems called rhizomes, sending up upright shoots that can reach about 2-3 feet tall. The golden-yellow flowers are quite showy, measuring about 1-2 inches across, and sit atop sturdy stems above distinctive heart-shaped leaves. It's actually a garden escape from Europe that occasionally pops up in New England's wild spaces.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow daisy-like flowers, 1-2 inches across, with many narrow petals radiating from a yellow center disc. The petals feel thin and delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped basal leaves that feel soft and somewhat fuzzy. The leaves at the base of the plant are larger and more pronounced than any that climb the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems growing 2-3 feet tall from spreading underground rhizomes. Plants often form small colonies over time as the rhizomes spread.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright green stems that feel firm and slightly hairy when you run your fingers along them. Usually unbranched or sparsely branched.

habitat: Look for leopard's-bane in semi-shaded areas like woodland edges, old gardens, and disturbed sites where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers moist, rich soils and can sometimes be found near old homesites or abandoned gardens. This European native is quite rare in New England's wild spaces, making any sighting noteworthy.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers bloom in late spring to early summer, creating cheerful golden displays. New heart-shaped leaves emerge fresh and green.
seasonality.summer: Flowers may continue into early summer, followed by fluffy seed heads. Foliage remains green and lush in favorable conditions.
seasonality.fall: Seeds disperse and leaves begin to yellow and die back. The plant starts preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes. No above-ground parts visible, making identification impossible during dormant season.

funFact: Despite its fearsome name suggesting it could take down big cats, leopard's-bane is actually a favorite food of deer and rabbits, who munch on it with no ill effects whatsoever!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for other yellow daisy-family flowers, but the distinctive heart-shaped basal leaves are the giveaway. Remember: heart-shaped leaves at the base = leopard's-bane, while most other yellow daisies have narrow or differently shaped leaves.
contextualKnowledge: This plant represents one of many old European garden flowers that occasionally 'jump the fence' into wild areas. The dramatic name reflects medieval superstitions about plant powers that have no basis in reality.
compareHints: Leopard's-bane is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other yellow daisy-family flowers like black-eyed Susans or goldenrods, leopard's-bane stands out with its distinctively heart-shaped basal leaves and its preference for shadier, moister spots rather than sunny fields.
